belief: People only feel sorry for me.
origins: Pity can feel patronizing: a head tilt, extra helpfulness, lowered expectations. Over time, we may shut out all kindness to avoid being pitied.
teaches: Jesus had compassion and also treated people as full persons: “Do you want to get well?” (John 5:6), He asked, and He said, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” Peter said to the lame man, “What I have I give you,” and then took him by the right hand. Compassion and respect go together. Not everyone gets it right, but many act from love. “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.” You can invite people to relate as equals.
self_statements: They see me as a charity case.
errors: Believing people either respect me or pity me.
Predicting that people will see only my condition.
Feeling pitied and concluding I am not respected.
questions: Who treats me as an equal?
What do I want people to see?
How can I invite a different kind of relationship?
What do I give back in friendship?
What did Jesus’ and Peter’s example show about compassion and respect?
What is one conversation where I could be more direct?
truth: People’s kindness can come from love, and I can invite respect by sharing what I want them to see. Jesus shows compassion that respects, and I can look for friendships of equals.
hw_truths: Jesus treated people as whole persons.
I give as well as receive.
log: Each week, note one interaction where you felt respected.
actions: Write who treats you as an equal.
Tell a friend how to help.
Encourage, pray for, or listen to others.
prayer: Lord, I want to be seen, not pitied. Teach me to receive kindness and invite respect, and send friends who see all of me. Amen.
